standard.title: Language and images create meaning in literature
standard.description: discuss how language and images are used to create characters, settings and events in literature by First Nations Australian, and wide-ranging Australian and world authors and illustrators
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can share ideas about stories, poems and images in literature, reflecting on experiences (AC9EFLE01). They have not yet discussed specifically how language choices and image choices work to construct characters, settings and events, or engaged with the diversity of literature from First Nations Australian, Australian and world authors.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students discuss how language and images are used to create characters, settings and events in literature from First Nations Australian, wide-ranging Australian and world authors and illustrators.

nodes.label: Characters are constructed through language and image
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can discuss how an author or illustrator uses specific words or images to create a character — what they look like, how they feel, what kind of person or creature they are.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two language or image choices in a text and explain what each tells the reader about a character.
nodes.typical_width: Discuss how authors use word choices (describing words, dialogue, actions) and illustrators use image choices (appearance, expression, colour) to create characters, using specific examples from familiar texts.
wider: Compare how the same type of character (e.g. an animal with human qualities) is created differently across two texts from different authors or cultures
Discuss how characters in literature by First Nations Australian authors and illustrators are depicted, exploring what the choices tell us about the character and their world

response_modes.reason: Students need to encounter diverse author and illustrator choices — not just one familiar style — to understand that character construction is a crafted decision, not a natural consequence. Texts from different cultural contexts make this especially visible.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Comparing character construction across texts by First Nations Australian authors and wide-ranging world authors is rich — it surfaces how cultural perspective shapes what details are foregrounded and what character qualities are valued.
success_criteria: Student identifies at least two specific language or image choices and links each to what it tells the reader about the character
Student uses the language of author/illustrator craft (e.g. 'the author chose... to show that...')

nodes.label: Settings are created through detail
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can discuss how authors and illustrators use language and images to create settings — where and when stories take place.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one language or image choice that creates a sense of place or time in a text, and describe the setting it creates.
nodes.typical_width: Discuss how authors use descriptive language and illustrators use visual details (colour, scale, perspective) to create settings, including whether settings feel real or imagined.
wider: Compare settings in texts from Australian and world authors — discuss how setting reflects the author's cultural context
Discuss whether a setting feels realistic or imagined and what specific choices create that effect
success_criteria: Student describes the setting of a text and identifies at least one language or image choice that creates it
Student states whether the setting seems realistic or imagined and gives a reason

nodes.label: Events unfold through language and image choices
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can discuss how authors and illustrators use language and images to depict events — what happens, how it happens, and why it matters.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify how at least one event in a text is conveyed through both words and images, and describe what each contributes.
nodes.typical_width: Discuss how events are depicted through language (action verbs, dialogue, description) and images (sequence, expression, movement), including how the two modes work together to create the full event.
wider: Explore how events in texts by First Nations Australian authors may be depicted in ways that differ from familiar narrative conventions
Examine how the same event depicted with different language or image choices would create a different reader experience

response_modes.reason: Events require students to coordinate understanding of character and setting — events happen to characters in settings. This node integrates the prior two nodes into a full discussion of how literature uses all its resources together.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Exploring how events might be depicted differently with different choices — and how First Nations texts may depict events in culturally distinct ways — opens genuinely rich territory for critical reading and cultural understanding.
success_criteria: Student describes an event and explains how both words and images contribute to the reader's understanding of it
Student identifies at least one specific choice (language or image) that shapes how the event feels to the reader
